rv.q: After an already-legendary Off Broadway debut at the Perelman Arts Center in 2024, this production—under the chosen name Cats: The Jellicle Ball–has now re-inhabited Broadway, where it remains a categorical triumph.
You’d have to be a real stickler for tradition to begrudge Jellicle Ball its innovations, and one suspects even the stickliest will find joy in the tunes and story that remain in this show’s DNA.
For the 40 or so minutes before it comes fully into itself, “Cats: The Jellicle Ball” is merely wonderful.
And yet, in placing new context and bodies inside the suit of ’80s excess, The Jellicle Ball reinvents it.
"Cats: The Jellicle Ball" just might become the next much-needed, must-see touring show from the House of Broadway.
What those outsiders have achieved with The Jellicle Ball is a revival in the fullest sense of the word.
And this bawdy crowd-pleaser at least has the courage of its crackpot convictions.
Trip Cullman oversees a sharp production that will leave you in stitches, anchored by Ehrenreich’s delicious performance as a man unafraid to be insufferable.
Cats: The Jellicle Ball's nervy fun, total sincerity, and embrace of over-the-top theatricality are already reason enough for the curious cat to check it out.
It is precisely all that history, deeply felt in this momentous staging, that makes both Moore and this production so otherworldly.
It's a transcendent, glitter-drenched revival that breaks all the rules of what Broadway can be – and in turn, creates something that is utterly extraordinary.
The spectacle of Jellicle Ball is intoxicating for all who enter and give themselves over to the glamor.
Not only is this Cats different from any you have ever seen before, it is the most dynamic musical show to be seen in New York right now.

CATS: The Jellicle Ball is an absolute trove of riches, filled with wonderful moments that bring together then and now while keeping everything fresh and alive, even for those totally unfamiliar with ballroom culture.
That sense of joy saturates every aspect of the production, from Omari Wiles and Arturo Lyons’s exuberant, sinuous choreography to Qween Jean’s characteristically vivid costumes
This irresistible revival isn’t your grandma’s Cats; but in many ways, it is the truest version of the musical yet.

The show’s book, adapted from T.S. Eliot’s rather twee “Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats,” remains completely intact (and essentially nonsensical), while Webber’s sometimes catchy, sometimes indulgent score is also performed in its entirety (if not always with good enunciation), all off which leads to a longish running time (as does an extend...

Artistically, the fresh interpretation not only offers the possibility of a renewed life and a new audience for this overly familiar 45-year-old show; it suggests how the art form as a whole can be reinvigorated.
In fact, the only thing that makes this "Cats" worth watching is the ballroom environment of high-and-low drag that gets dropped like a bottle of Pooph onto Lloyd Webber's litter box of a musical.
Reimagining Andrew Lloyd Webber’s “Cats” through the lens of Ballroom culture and voguing is brilliant.
The introduction of ballroom and 'house' culture breathes fresh energy and a human-scaled depth to the material.
Cats: The Jellicle Ball is a fine tribute to ballroom.
There is not enough glitter in the world to cover up how inane Cats truly is.
Swapping out cat ears for couture and the junkyard for the runway, this revival redefines itself and sharply recontextualizes the feline festival with a little less mystique and a lot more sparkle.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this ballroom-infused reimagining as a joyous, inventive reinvention that rescues the divisive musical with fierce choreography and queer celebration, though a few find the opulence excessive or question the concept's depth.

sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name Center Orchestra rows D-K as the house sweet spot; Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang does not begin cutting the stage picture until row K, so D-K sits entirely in front of the overhang line while still clearing the shallow front-row rake. SeatPlan editors specifically advise skipping rows A-C because the Broadhurst stage pushes action to the sides that front-row patrons miss.

Broadhurst's mezzanine overhang begins at row K and, per Headout and SeatPlan, 'visibly cuts into the top of the stage by row R' - specifically blocking projections and anything that plays high. The rake in these rear orchestra rows is also called out as shallow, compounding the loss of vertical stage picture.

SeatPlan specifically flags the Broadhurst's Left and Right Boxes as overhanging far-aisle orchestra seats around rows D-F, cutting off the corresponding side of the stage, and the three elevated boxes themselves 'sit at quite sharp angles' with unfixed chairs. Headout adds that double-digit seats near the aisle get only partial views of the stage.

Multiple sources (Headout, SeatPlan, NewYorkTheatreGuide) call Center Mezzanine rows A-B the second-best location in the house. The Broadhurst's front mezzanine ledge has no railing, so shorter patrons aren't blocked - a Broadhurst-specific quirk noted by both SeatPlan and Headout. Because there is no balcony above, front-mezz rows have zero overhang.

SeatPlan calls Center Mezzanine rows C-F the value pick - 'enough rake to see over the top of heads' at sub-premium pricing - and because Broadhurst has no balcony above, the rear mezzanine is not overhung itself. The back four rows are slightly shorter with a decent rake, and a Tripadvisor reviewer (Apr 2024) reported a 'crystal clear view' from the last row of the mezzanine.

vr.q: Cats the Jellicle Ball is a masterpiece and you should not miss it.
